newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's Soriana gears up for competition.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Soriana gears up for competition.

text.p: The most telling sign that retailer Organizacion Soriana SA's traditional grip on northern Mexico may be slipping is an ultra-modern, gigantic supermarket being built here by H.E.B. Grocery Co.
The sleek, art deco-style superstore, due to open early next year, is the first foray into Mexico by the Texas-based chain, which plans eventually to open five stores in the Monterrey area.

H.E.B. follows other retailers, local and foreign, who are setting up shop in northern Mexico, where an export boom has created just about the only healthy market of consumers in a country still licking its wounds from the 1994 peso crash.
Mexico's Cifra, the country's biggest retail company, plans to open up a handful superstores within a year as part of its joint venture with U.S.-based Wal-Mart.
And France's Carrefour also is eyeing northern Mexico for places to set up its successful superstores, analysts say.

The moves have caused some industry watchers to wonder whether Soriana will be able to maintain what have been the highest profit margins of any Mexican retailer -- margins that have doubled Soriana's stock price since the start of the year.
"We know the competition is coming and we are ready for it," Soriana's chief financial officer Javier Lozano said on Friday during a retail conference here.

Until now, the Monterrey-based chain has dominated this area's lonely retail landscape, setting up dozens of single- format hypermarkets. It targets low and middle-income consumers with mostly food items and few high-priced imports.

Soriana was one of the few Mexican retailers to emerge from the devaluation largely unscathed. A mostly cash-only expansion philosophy left the company with little debt, free to grow while other retailers were scaling back.

The retailer has opened three new stores this year and plans on two more, bringing its total to 61 outlets. It wants to open seven new stores next year, and possibly more the year after depending on cash flow, Lozano said.
Despite expansion, the company has managed to reduce its total debt further, from 185 million pesos at the start of the year to a current 72 million pesos.
Lozano admitted competition is likely to squeeze the company's margins. And he said he expects little help from the Mexican economy in helping create a bigger pie for all competitors.
"The recovery for the individual consumer will not happen in the short-run, even in the medium-run. Consumers suffered a serious setback and the recovery will be gradual," Lozano said.
But the company does have several things in its favor, such as its regional focus that allows it to have economies of scale and low distribution costs.

Soriana is positioned to take advantage of a weak economy. Northern Mexicans will no longer drive a few hours to the U.S. border for shopping or buy imports here for at least a few years, two trends that were booming before the devaluation.

"We offer products that are geared to the (middle and low) economic level -- functional products that aren't necessarily the latest trend but are cheaper than what they can buy in the United States," Lozano said.
The company expects the Mexican consumer to remain wary of credit offered by department stores even after the effects of the devaluation wear off, he said.
Industry trends also favor superstores like Soriana and H.E.B. versus traditional outdoor markets or Mom-and-Pop stores.
"Growth in our stores sales should more than offset the fall in margins," he said.
During September, Soriana has seen overall sales to grow by about 13 percent and same-store sales to rise some 9 percent compared to the same month of 1995, according to Lozano.
-- Mexico City newsroom 525 7289565
